name: Powdery Mildew
description: A common fungal disease that coats leaves in white, flour-like patches. It thrives in warm days, cool nights, and poor air circulation.
symptoms: White or grey powdery spots on leaves and stems
treatment: Remove and bin heavily infected leaves (do not compost)
Spray with a potassium bicarbonate or diluted neem oil solution every 7 days
Apply a sulfur-based fungicide for persistent cases
prevention: Space plants for good air flow
Water at the base, in the morning

name: Early Blight
description: Caused by Alternaria fungi, early blight produces target-like brown rings on older, lower leaves first and slowly works upward.
treatment: Prune affected lower leaves with sterilised shears
Apply a copper or chlorothalonil-based fungicide
Mulch to stop soil splashing onto leaves
prevention: Stake plants to keep foliage off the ground

name: Late Blight
description: A fast-spreading, destructive disease (the cause of the Irish potato famine). It can wipe out plants within days in cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked patches on leaves
White fuzzy growth on leaf undersides
Brown, firm rot on fruit or tubers
treatment: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately — bag them, don't compost
Protect nearby plants with a copper-based fungicide
Harvest any healthy fruit or tubers early
prevention: Monitor closely during cool, humid spells

name: Leaf Mold
description: A humidity-loving fungus common in greenhouses and polytunnels. It mostly affects leaves, reducing the plant's vigour.
symptoms: Pale yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to brown velvety mould underneath
treatment: Remove affected leaves
Increase ventilation and reduce humidity below 85%
Apply a suitable fungicide if spreading

name: Bacterial Spot
description: Caused by Xanthomonas bacteria, it creates small dark lesions on leaves and fruit, spreading via splashing water.
symptoms: Spots may merge and leaves turn yellow
treatment: Remove infected foliage
Apply copper-based bactericide early
Avoid working with plants when they are wet
prevention: Drip irrigate rather than overhead water

name: Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
description: A virus spread by whiteflies. There is no cure once infected, so controlling the insects is essential.
symptoms: Severely stunted growth and few fruits
treatment: Remove and destroy infected plants to protect others
Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps or insecticidal soap
There is no chemical cure for the virus itself
prevention: Use insect netting over young plants

name: Black Spot
description: The most common rose disease. Black spots with fringed edges appear on leaves, which then yellow and fall.
symptoms: Round black spots with feathery margins
treatment: Pick off and bin infected leaves, including fallen ones
Spray with a rose fungicide or neem oil weekly
Prune to open up the centre of the bush
prevention: Water early in the day at soil level

name: Downy Mildew
description: A water-mould disease that turns leaves yellow with grey-purple fuzz underneath. It spreads quickly in humid conditions.
symptoms: Grey-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides
treatment: Remove infected plants or leaves promptly
Improve air circulation and reduce leaf wetness
Use a copper-based fungicide as a preventive

name: Root Rot
description: Usually caused by overwatering and poor drainage, which suffocate the roots and allow rot fungi to take hold.
symptoms: Yellowing, wilting leaves despite moist soil
treatment: Unpot the plant and rinse the roots
Trim all mushy, brown roots with sterile scissors
Repot in fresh, well-draining mix in a pot with drainage holes
prevention: Water only when the top of the soil is dry
Always use pots with drainage holes
Use a chunky, airy potting mix

name: Spider Mites
description: Tiny sap-sucking arachnids that thrive in dry air. Large colonies produce fine webbing and can weaken plants quickly.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckling on leaves
Delicate webbing under leaves and at stems
Leaves become dull, bronze, and dry
treatment: Isolate the plant from others
Rinse leaves thoroughly, especially undersides
Spray with insecticidal soap or neem oil every 5–7 days for 3 weeks

name: Leaf Spot
description: A group of fungal and bacterial infections that cause brown or black spots on foliage, usually encouraged by wet leaves.
symptoms: Brown or black spots, sometimes with yellow halos
Spots merging into larger dead patches
treatment: Remove affected leaves
Keep foliage dry when watering
Apply a copper fungicide if the problem spreads
prevention: Water the soil, not the leaves

name: Leaf Scorch
description: Damage caused by too much direct sun, heat, or sudden exposure to brighter light. Not infectious, but scorched tissue won't recover.
symptoms: Bleached, white, or brown crispy patches
Damage on the side facing the light
treatment: Move the plant out of harsh direct sun
Trim badly scorched leaves for appearance
Water deeply if the soil is bone dry
prevention: Acclimatise plants to brighter light gradually
Use sheer curtains for south-facing windows
Keep plants away from hot glass

name: Mealybugs
description: Soft-bodied insects covered in white, cottony wax. They cluster in leaf joints and suck sap, leaving sticky honeydew behind.
treatment: Dab bugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% isopropyl alcohol
Spray with insecticidal soap weekly
Repeat treatment for at least 4 weeks to break the life cycle

name: Nitrogen Deficiency
description: A lack of nitrogen causes older leaves to turn pale yellow as the plant moves nutrients to new growth.
symptoms: Uniform yellowing of older, lower leaves
treatment: Apply a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertiliser
Top-dress with compost or well-rotted manure
Re-check in 2 weeks for greener new growth
prevention: Feed regularly during the growing season
Rotate with legumes in vegetable beds
